posts.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
posts.text: There have been questions about why the /ask page ( https://news.ycombinator.com/ask ) was running dry of Ask HN posts - e.g.: Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments) Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments) I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs. p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

comments.text: That’s pretty funny! I’ve seen optimizations like this for reporting systems where rather than taking the top N item matching filter X, they cheat by taking the top M (where M > N) items and then filter it client side to N items matching filter X. As long as the results are enough to populate the page you don’t notice the difference and it’s usually faster as you reuse the prior ranking. But if not, you get this exact situation.

posts.title: Ask HN: For professional Mathematicians –- about your career in the future
posts.text: Hi friends, genuine question. We all see that top notch Mathematicians can use LLM to prove world class results in a relatively short time of period. OK I admit some of the results are not verified yet, but please hear me. Neither do I know how much “brain” is human and how much is the LLM, because we don’t see the prompts. My question is: what do you think about your career in the future? Please hear me out. In the current world, the way you become a Mathematician, is to get good scores, go to schools, take PHD and then professorship. There may be middle steps like postdoctoral or industry experience, but that’s the general way to do it. And the way that schools judge professors, if I understand correctly, is more about how much results you can get —- ofc if you can obtain big grants then the better, but most of you can’t do that, so I assume that it’s more about the papers. You also teach but that’s not as big as the research. For now, there are a lot of smaller problems left to solve, and since world class Mathematicians tend to devote their life to one world class problem, there are plenty of food for everyone. Does the above make sense? This leads me to the question of: if the future of getting proofs is to prompt with an LLM or whatever AI solution, and it is apparent that world class Mathematicians can prove more conjectures or whatever than they ever can dream without LLM, why do schools need mediocre Mathematicians? I’m not trying to belittle you, but I’m trying to figure out career paths for my son, and I need to understand the impact of AI to all career paths. Again, I iterate, if one world class Mathematicians can prompt through many problems in their lifetime, we face two possibilities: 1. LLMs are good at solving problems but not good at asking new questions, so eventually we have few questions to crack, so the world doesn’t really need that many Mathematicians. 2. LLM is equally good at asking new questions. Well again I don’t see why the school needs to hire so many Mathematicians. Again, I believe LLM is merely the tool here, you still need the Mathematicians to do the thinking —- this does NOT contradict what I wrote. Of course, there is another part of your work, that is to teach Mathematics. But I’m not sure that is unique to humans. Maybe LLM can do that too. It just needs more training on that because so far the training is more on proving things, not teaching things. I want to iterate a third time, that I’m not belittling you. You are smarter than me, so please help me understand the situation. This is more about employment, not about interests —- if one is interested in Math, sure go ahead and learn the hell out of it —- but persuading people to pay you to do that is different. Thanks in advance.

posts.title: Ask HN: Are the trades a safe career transition?
posts.text: I am a software guy. Engineering degree but not PEng. Im thinking of jumping ship because i dont see much of a future in the career. Ai has me a little discouraged I need a few decades of at least mild security to get to retirement... Are the trades safe? Im worried about homeowners and companies ending up with robots that do all those tasks. Not next year obviously, but it could happen before the career change fully pays off And if not the trades, then what is a better bet?

comments.text: If you look at a graph of the US economy, and remove software and data centers, there’s basically no growth. Don’t leave software. AI will change your job, but it won’t replace you, not even in multiple decades. Be strategic about the kinds of software roles you get into. Look for niches with stability. Look to go toward highly regulated software niches. For example, I work in an area where it would be impossible to remove manual testers due to certain regulations. Software work for government where you must be a US citizen or you must do specific things manually could be another example. I also think some areas are going to be more insulated from AI disruption. I think ops and security have more stability. Anything that requires more judgment and less “take inputs and turn them into outputs.” Moving from an upper middle class career track to something you can get into without a high school diploma is a mistake. In many trades you’re competing with dudes who are working under the table and aren’t even documented. Even if you’re not, they’re mostly hard on your body, and some aren’t even immune from automation.

comments.text: I’ve never worked as a professional tradesman, but I’ve done quite a bit of that type of work. It’s hard. It’s hard on your body in ways that will become more of an issue as you age. It’s also, imho, very satisfying work. But it’s tough. And even though you might look at your last plumbing bill and say “damn, that would be good money!” the reality is that very few in the trades will bring all of that home themselves. As for AI in the software field… I’ve watched the people around me. Some of them are doing good work with AI. And what they all have in common is serious skill and experience predating AI. What it looks like from my seat is that AI in software dev and related fields is absolutely a force multiplier… but only for people who already know what they’re doing. So as a few other people have said, don’t be too hasty to jump ship. There may yet be some good opportunities. Btw, having said all of that, my AI use is limited to summarizing searches and assisting on code review. I’m personally quite “anti AI” and close enough to retirement that if eventually I can’t keep up without going all-in, I’m ok with being fired. Love my job and the people I work with, though.

comments.text: AI is definitely changing things a lot in the field, but don't discount the massive change in how cheap money was during ZIRP and how expensive it became after ZIRP finally ended. This was coincidentally around the same time the layoffs in big tech started, which was before AI really had any meaningful impact. When money is cheap it is a lot easier for companies to hire, and when money suddenly stops being cheap it is a lot harder. In particular, large discontinuities in economic conditions, which we just experienced recently post-covid, always produce downturns in affected industries (which is distinct from the first order aspect of how expensive money is). So I think even ignoring AI we could expect several years of down-ness and reorganization followed by a recovery. I don't think we can even tell this point if AI will reduce demand for developers. The economy for software might be even worse right now if the AI developments hadn't happened when they did, there was an insane hiring spree during COVID and even before that the industry employment-side was growing at a probably unsustainable pace.

posts.title: Ask HN: How to manage "crown jewel" files?
posts.text: I’m looking to understand how organizations manage crown jewel type documents, designs, plans, strategies etc. Files that are not for general consumption across a company, but rather the sensitive material in a company that needs actual protection and access controls. I’m struggling with how to handle this properly for a growing venture. Thanks HN. - Windows shares with permissions? - Some form of content management system? - SharePoint? - Maybe unmanaged on specific users’ PCs (not great but probably the default in smaller organizations?) - Something else. What options are folks using that I may be overlooking?

comments.text: IMHO: combine 2 things: "Role based access control" (RBAC) + "Principle of Least Privilege" (PLoP) You could add 3rd and 4th things: "single sign on" (SSO) and "biometric authentication" (biometrics). SSO is how you make RBAC and PLoP work together, and is required for biometrics to work effectively, too. Gating SSO with biometrics is the only way to make reasonably sure the person using that computer or phone is actually the person who has been given that role's access, and not someone else who, you know, has access to their devices, password, or some other way of getting into their account. If you do RBAC + PLoP + SSO + biometrics, and you hired people you can trust to not be silly, then you just have to think about what other software is running on their machines. Security is in layers and you can go as deep as you want to.

If you are so inclined and depending on your use case, you can encrypt before upload and store the crypto primitives elsewhere (Hashicorp Vault/OpenBao, corp password vault, etc) to decrypt, depending on how often the artifacts are accessed and/or modified as an additional access control layer. comments.text: Something I expect from a senior engineer is the ability to take a failure without placing blame, and turn it into an opportunity to improve things while also taking actions to prevent the same failure mode from occuring. Gaps on resumes are not unique to you. People have unexpected unemployment for many reasons. If you treat that gap like it's a negative thing, and as you say "explain it", I'm going to think there's something negative behind it. Instead treat it as a matter of fact, then present the opportunities you took in the mean time. What makes someone with a gap stand out to is how they "sell" that gap to me. What did you do in that time to improve yourself, keep your skills sharp, grow as a human being? How are you going to show me that you still have passion and drive to remain in this industry? Also, reframe your thinking. You are not an engineer looking for work, you are a sales person selling an engineer. Take time to understand what qualities in an engineer they want beyond mere skills and experience. For example, you don't sell a used car by starting with "It's been on the road 15 years". You try to appeal to what the buyer is looking for. Do they want an easily customizable sports car, a reliable commuter, fuel efficiency? Hiring teams are buyers, you're the product. There's a lot of other boring sounding, but good advice in this thread, such as networking. Networking should not just be about meeting people who may be hiring, it's also about keeping a pulse on the industry and social engagement beyond just talking within online forums. Go to free conferences, meet people, engage. It makes it a lot easier to interview. Whatever you do, don't lie, and I recommend blocking anyone who recommend you do.

comments.text: As a manager, I have a rule for people joining my team. You can’t make big changes in your first few months. This doesn’t mean our code base is amazing or that you are wrong… it’s simply that you have to really learn the business and the code base before you really understand what the priorities are. I tell people to write down things that they don’t like and then a few months in, we can circle back and decide if they are worth changing. It’s easy to have a myopic viewpoint when you don’t fully understand how things fit together or what the business priorities are. Now, I am not doubting that you have come up with a better pattern. But there is merit in having consistency within a code base. Sometimes doing things the same way across modules is easier to maintain, even if it is suboptimal. If you are new to a codebase, my advice is to stick to the current conventions. When you are three or four months into the job, and you have earned some credibility, then it is OK to circle back and suggest some refactors.

When I'm working on a project for some time ($JOB), I usually end up writing little utilities and makefiles to speed up common tasks. Especially if they are some things I need to do on a regular basis. Sometimes it doesn't pay out in the end. But the whole flow is smoother and thus more delightful. Old GUI used to have a lot of shortcuts (Just checked and QT in KDE stil supports Alt based navigation (I forgot the exact name)), but now it's just icons and non visible keybindings. Also most TUI can easily shell out to other utilities making integration easy. To recap: I code better when I have smoother workflow, which means easy access to the information I need now (next error from the last run, docs for the current function,...). IDE help but they're usually overfitted to one project style and languages. I ship quicker when I can automate the whole workflow to a series of actions and succinct results I can quickly review. comments.text: The comments so far appear to be tackling external recruiters however I think you're actually asking about internal recruiters so I'll focus on that. Context: My career started in software engineering before moving into recruitment. I spent a few years agency-side (external) but the majority of my career has been internal (including with a few YC companies). I have about ~15yrs of experience ranging from tech recruiter to Global VP of Talent. Assessing recruiter skills (just like assessing an engineer's skills) varies from company to company. One of the most common metrics is 'time to hire' which is essentially a measure of how long it takes to go from a vacancy going live, to having someone in the seat. Ultimately that is the most useful measure because an ineffective recruiter will take much longer to fill an open role. For me, the next most important measure was essentially a hiring manager NPS. I appreciate you might assume that the candidate NPS is more important however I've found that people you've just given a job to tend to only provide positive feedback on the experience so it's a bit redundant. Another critical measure of efficacy for me is the interview success rate ratio. We'd look at every stage of our hiring pipeline and measure the pass/fail ratio with the goal being as close to a 50/50 split as possible. Having a balance is important because if everyone you interview is good enough to get through to the next stage then either your process is lacking rigour or your standards aren't high enough! This measure also tends to counter the whole "throw shit at the wall and see what sticks" approach. When you're an internal recruiter, one of the biggest values you add to a business is reducing the time the business spends on recruitment so less time interviewing poor quality candidates is critical. On the point of retention rates; I generally don't hold my recruiters accountable for that. Naturally we pay attention to any obvious negative trends but broadly speaking, it's the recruiters job to identify and attract good people, it's the hiring team and hiring managers responsibility to assess them and on-board them properly. It's my job to help the hiring team and hiring managers get better at retention. Happy to answer any other questions you have!
